findings.sourceEvidence: "Deleveraging Trigger Period" means any period (other than a Second Deleveraging Trigger Period, determined without regard to clause (ii) of the definition thereof) after the Effective Date from and including any day on which the Administrative Agent determines that the Prevailing Market Value of the Collateral is less than 70% of the Initial Prevailing Market Value to but excluding the first day thereafter when the Administrative Agent determines that the Prevailing Market Value of the Collateral is equal to or greater than the Initial Prevailing Market Value.
findings.proposedIrEvidence: calculationExpression.triggerCondition = COMPARE(PrevailingMarketValue LT 0.7*InitialPrevailingMarketValue) with no AND/NOT clause excluding periods that are a Second Deleveraging Trigger Period; "Second Deleveraging Trigger Period" only appears in dependsOnTerms metadata, not in the actual boolean logic.
findings.verifierReasoning: The source text explicitly carves Second Deleveraging Trigger Periods out of the Deleveraging Trigger Period definition ('other than a Second Deleveraging Trigger Period'). Because a Second Deleveraging Trigger Period (PMV < 50% of Initial) is a numeric subset of the Deleveraging Trigger Period test (PMV < 70% of Initial), the proposed IR's trigger condition - which omits any exclusion of SDT - would evaluate TRUE for Deleveraging Trigger Period even when the Collateral value has fallen below 50% of Initial (i.e., during a Second Deleveraging Trigger Period), contrary to the source's clear mutual-exclusivity intent. A downstream consumer computing 'is a Deleveraging Trigger Period currently in effect?' from this IR alone could get a different, wrong answer versus the source in any scenario where PMV is below 50% of Initial (e.g., PMV = 40% of Initial): source says only SDT applies; proposed IR's formula for DTP alone would also say TRUE. This affects which Applicable Margin and which LTV Table column (Deleveraging Trigger Period vs Second Deleveraging Trigger Period, which carry materially different Liquidation/Top Up/Initial/Release LTV percentages) should be used.

findings.sourceEvidence: "LTV Table" means the following table: [Liquidation LTV: 80%/75%/70%; Top Up LTV: 70%/65%/60%; Initial LTV: 60%/55%/50%; Release LTV: 50%/45%/40%, across the three period columns 'Other than any Deleveraging/Second Deleveraging Trigger Period', 'During any Deleveraging Trigger Period', and 'During any Second Deleveraging Trigger Period']
findings.proposedIrEvidence: definitions[termName='LTV Table'].calculationExpression = null; sufficiency = "COMPLETE"; dependsOnTerms = ["Liquidation LTV","Top Up LTV","Initial LTV","Release LTV",...], each of which (Liquidation LTV, Top Up LTV, Initial LTV, Release LTV) is itself represented with calculationExpression.kind="UNSUPPORTED" and sufficiency="PARTIAL".
findings.verifierReasoning: None of the twelve actual percentage values in the LTV Table (80/75/70, 70/65/60, 60/55/50, 50/45/40) are captured anywhere in the proposed IR - every sub-definition that would carry those numbers is marked UNSUPPORTED/PARTIAL. Despite this, the LTV Table definition itself is marked sufficiency COMPLETE with a null calculationExpression, i.e., it claims full representation of a rule whose entire substantive content (the numeric thresholds governing margin calls, top-up, release and liquidation of Bitcoin collateral) is missing. This is exactly the confident-but-wrong pattern that deserves the most scrutiny: a reviewer relying on the LTV Table's COMPLETE flag could wrongly conclude the thresholds are captured somewhere in the IR when they are not captured at all, materially affecting any downstream capacity/compliance determination that depends on actual LTV percentages (e.g., is a Blocking Event triggered because Actual LTV Ratio >= Top Up LTV?).

findings.irPath: definitions[termName='Early Termination Fee'].calculationExpression (and definitions[termName='LTV Breach Notice'])
findings.sourceEvidence: "Early Termination Fee" means ... an amount ... equal to the product of (i) the principal amount of the Loan being repaid or prepaid, multiplied by (ii) the Applicable Margin, multiplied by (iii) the applicable Day Count Fraction. / "LTV Breach Notice" means a notice delivered upon the Actual LTV Ratio being equal to or in excess of the Liquidation LTV pursuant to Section 2.03(h)...
findings.sourceCitation: Section 1.01, definitions of "Early Termination Fee" and "LTV Breach Notice"
findings.proposedIrEvidence: Early Termination Fee.sufficiency = "COMPLETE" although its operand DEFINED_TERM_REFERENCE("Applicable Margin") points to a definition whose own calculationExpression.kind = "UNSUPPORTED" and sufficiency = "PARTIAL"; LTV Breach Notice.sufficiency = "COMPLETE" although it depends on "Liquidation LTV", whose calculationExpression.kind = "UNSUPPORTED" and sufficiency = "PARTIAL".
findings.verifierReasoning: Early Termination Fee and LTV Breach Notice are each marked fully COMPLETE, but each is arithmetically/logically dependent on an upstream term (Applicable Margin, Liquidation LTV respectively) that the IR itself admits it failed to formalize (UNSUPPORTED/PARTIAL). A consumer cannot actually compute the Early Termination Fee or evaluate an LTV Breach Notice trigger using only what this IR resolves, despite the COMPLETE label suggesting otherwise. Whether this rises to a fully material defect depends on how downstream tooling propagates sufficiency status, but at minimum the COMPLETE claim on these definitions is not honestly supported by their own dependency graph.
